text: With a task and a candidate model picked last lesson, this is where the capstone gets its hands dirty: building the actual SFT dataset. Every later lesson in this capstone inherits whatever quality problems go unnoticed here, so it's worth doing carefully.

However you source examples — writing them by hand, adapting an existing dataset, or using a stronger model to draft and then reviewing and correcting — the goal is prompt-response pairs representative of what you want the fine-tuned model to do well. A few hundred to a couple thousand well-chosen examples is realistic for a capstone. Quality and style consistency matter far more here than raw volume.

Three things catch most dataset problems. Prompt masking, so loss is only computed on response tokens, not the prompt — confirm this rather than assuming it, especially with a custom formatting function. Length filtering, since a handful of outlier-long examples can dominate a small dataset's effective epoch. And deduplication, because near-duplicate examples, common when generating drafts with a model, inflate the effective weight of just a few patterns.

Formatting matters as much as sourcing: build each example into messages and run them through the exact model's apply_chat_template, not a hand-rolled approximation — that mismatch is a common, hard-to-spot source of poor results. Then split off a held-out slice before any training happens, and don't look at it again until the evaluation lesson.

That held-out split is what makes the later evaluation honest: genuine performance on examples the model never trained on, not a number quietly computed on data it already memorized. Next up: running the actual fine-tune, with LoRA or QLoRA, on the dataset you just built.
